lines.text: This month, a little town in Ohio called Piqua just got rid of its mayor for approving a Meta data centre to be built there.
Data centres are big buildings full of computers that run all your AI.
They're very unpopular with the left wing who are concerned about the environmental impacts and very popular with the right wing who see big tech as the big economic growth machine at all costs.
And Gallup, it's a big business that does surveys, found people now object to having a data centre next to them more than they object to having a nuclear power plant next to them.
That's crazy.
So if you pay for AI at work or at home, could the midterm results in America push your bill up?
And where does AI get built when the town's residents say no to the big data centres?
Let's find out.
So I've been digging into Piqua all week, and honestly it's the whole AI story in one small town.
So Meta, the big social media giant wanted a data centre on the business park by the main road in this town.
And last year the mayor Jim Vetter said, yes, along with his council.
And then the neighbours started doing the maths.

A big data centre uses as much electricity as a small city so to feed one of these data centres the electricity company often has to build new lines and new power plants and the cost of those can end up on everyone's bill.

So picture opening up your electricity bill and it's just randomly gone up double and then you find out you're chipping in for the power lines to Facebook's new data centre and that's what people in Piqua were worried about so on the 3rd of November Piqua voted on two questions number one should we ban big data centres and it was yes resoundingly by two to one of its residents and the second one was should we sack the mayor and two of the councillors that backed this proposal and that one was even more that was 70% of the residents talk about a bad day at the office and Piqua wasn't a one-off Ballotpedia which tracks elections in the US counted 41 local votes on data centres just that day and then all but one the data centre lost now here's my favourite detail Meta's data centre was already being built by this point.

So Piqua now has a data centre going up in a town where its residents have banned the data centre Meta says it will work with local officials on what happens next which is You know their way of Facebooking their way out of the situation and saying we'll deal with it next time.
So And the backlash has rattled the biggest names too.
The two days after that vote OpenAI, ChatGPT's maker, made a promise that it would pay the full cost of the new power that its data centres would need.
That way the neighbours' bills don't go up.
Lovely promise.
It's also the exact same one it made back in January and the voters kept saying no anyway.
So what is everyone building AI doing about this?
Oracle, big software giant, they decided to skip the town's electricity altogether and it signed up for a whole fleet of gas power plants to power its own data centres.
so the neighbours promised to not use your electricity and then built a gas plant in your backyard.

and shockingly neighbours don't love a gas plant either others they're heading for the countryside Soluna which is a small energy firm builds small data centres right next to wind and solar farms and those farms often make more power than the cables can carry anyway.
So Soluna's data centres use it up on the spot with far fewer neighbours to annoy.
But a small data centre can only really run the AI tools that exist now and have in the past.
Building the next versions of AI, smarter AI, needs thousands of computers working together in one giant data centre in one place.
So you're right back to needing a little town like Piqua to say yes to this.
And then there's Apple.
Apple's going the other way entirely.
It's actually putting more AI on your phone, on the device.
On a newer iPhone, it can sum up a long email now without sending it anywhere.
No data centre, no power lines, no one having to vote on anything.
So the catch, a pocket-sized AI just does less.
It's great for that one email, but it's not great to run your whole business on.
So here's the whole story in one breath.
A town said no, a mayor got sacked, a data centre kept going up and the companies kept looking for ways around this.
And honestly I think the bigger question is who pays for this electricity and power.
When a town and their residents say no, the AI companies have to find their own power.
Think Oracle's gas plants or OpenAI's promise.
And I reckon that cost gets passed on to you either if you're a business owner or if you're a subscriber to these tools at your next AI tool renewal.

I've seen in the last three days alone, I've seen in the last week alone, three instances of of companies trying to get me to switch my plan to a different pricing model and I can see that if I'm switching I'm going to get loads of new credits to start with but in the long term I'm going to be paying a lot more and that's how they're trying to get old contracts on new price points that favor them.
And as for Meta's data centre, it's still going up in that town that just banned it.
I'd love to be a fly on the wall at Piqua's next council meeting.

so the next time you renew an AI tool ask yourself two things which is what do those pricing terms actually mean in the long term and where are the data centres for the product being built because if it's in a town that's just said no that power bill is heading straight for my desk anyway.
The full story is at makeyourmindup.ai
